title: Time Passes · 6
paragraphs: Spring came without a single leaf to toss about. Bare and bright, like a virgin fierce in her chastity and scornful in her purity, she lay spread over the fields, wide-eyed and watchful, and not in the least concerned with what anyone looking at her might do or think.
[That May, Prue Ramsay, leaning on her father’s arm, was given away in marriage. Could anything have been more fitting? people asked. And how beautiful she looked, they added!]

As summer drew near and the evenings lengthened, the wakeful and the hopeful who walked the beach and stirred the pools began to have the strangest imaginings: of flesh turned into atoms that drove before the wind, of stars flashing in their hearts, of cliff, sea, cloud and sky gathered together on purpose so that, out there, they might assemble the scattered pieces of the vision within. In those mirrors, the minds of men—in those pools of uneasy water, where clouds are always turning and shadows forming—dreams persisted. Every gull, flower, tree, man and woman, even the white earth itself, seemed to declare (though, if you questioned it, it would at once take the words back) that good triumphs, that happiness prevails, that order rules; and it was impossible to resist this strange hint. It was just as impossible to resist the extraordinary urge to roam this way and that in search of some absolute good, some crystal of intensity, far removed from familiar pleasures and known virtues—something alien to the business of domestic life, single, hard, bright, like a diamond in the sand, that would make its owner safe. Spring, meanwhile, had grown gentler and more yielding. With her bees humming and her gnats dancing, she drew her cloak around her, veiled her eyes and turned her head aside, and among the passing shadows and small gusts of rain she seemed to have taken on some knowledge of human sorrow.
[That summer Prue Ramsay died of some illness connected with childbirth. It was a real tragedy, people said. Nobody, they said, had deserved happiness more.]

And now, in the summer heat, the wind once more sent its spies around the house. In the sunny rooms flies spun a web; weeds that had sprung up against the glass overnight tapped at the windowpane in a steady rhythm. When darkness came, the stroke of the Lighthouse—which in the dark had once laid itself across the carpet with such authority, tracing out its pattern—now arrived in the softer spring light, mixed with moonlight. It glided in gently, as if laying a caress, lingering in secret, looking, and coming lovingly back again. Yet in the very hush of that loving caress, as the long stroke leaned across the bed, the rock split apart; another fold of the shawl worked loose, and hung there, swaying. All through the short summer nights and long summer days, while the empty rooms seemed to murmur with echoes from the fields and the buzzing of flies, the long streamer stirred gently and swung without purpose. The sun, meanwhile, laid such stripes and bars across the rooms and filled them with so yellow a haze that when Mrs. McNab broke in and lurched about with her duster and broom, she looked like a tropical fish paddling its way through water pierced with sunbeams.

Yet however deeply the house might slumber and sleep, later that summer ominous sounds reached it, like hammer blows falling in a slow rhythm, muffled on felt. Their repeated shocks loosened the shawl further still and cracked the teacups. Every so often a glass tinkled in the cupboard, as though some giant voice had screamed so loud in its agony that even the tumblers standing inside a cupboard shook too. Then silence fell once more. And then, night after night—and sometimes in the full light of noon, when the roses were bright and the light printed its shape plainly on the wall—there seemed to drop into this silence, this indifference, this wholeness, the thud of something falling.
[A shell burst. In France twenty or thirty young men were blown up, and Andrew Ramsay was one of them. His death, mercifully, was instant.]

That season, people who had gone down to walk the beach and ask the sea and sky what message they carried, or what vision they confirmed, found something new to consider. Among the familiar signs of heaven’s generosity—sunset on the sea, the pale dawn, the rising moon, fishing boats against the moon, children throwing handfuls of grass at one another—there was something that did not fit with all this gaiety and calm. There was, for instance, a gray ship, the color of ash, that silently appeared and was gone; there was a purple stain on the smooth sea, as though something underneath had boiled and bled out of sight. These things broke into a scene built to call up the loftiest thoughts and lead to the most reassuring conclusions, and they stopped the walkers in their tracks. It was hard to pass over them calmly, to cancel out what they meant in the landscape; hard to keep walking by the sea and marveling that the beauty outside mirrored the beauty within.

Did Nature add her part to what man offered? Did she finish what he started? She looked on his misery with the same complacency, excused his meanness, and consented to his torture. So was that dream—of sharing, of completing, of finding an answer alone on the beach—nothing but a reflection in a mirror? And was the mirror nothing but the glassy film that forms on the surface in stillness, while the nobler powers lie sleeping below? Impatient and despairing, yet unwilling to leave (for beauty has her lures to offer, and her consolations), they could no longer pace the beach; contemplation had become unbearable; the mirror was broken.
[That spring Mr. Carmichael published a book of poems, and it turned out to be an unexpected success. People said the war had brought back their interest in poetry.]
